knowledge.text: The AIATSIS map (created 1996 by David R Horton for the Encyclopaedia of Aboriginal Australia) attempts to represent language, social or nation groups using published sources from the 18th century to 1994; it shows general locations of larger groupings, borders are deliberately blurred, some information is contested, and it is not suitable for native title or land claims.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: The AIATSIS map may not be cropped, overlaid, or have geospatial mapping added; reproduction requires Aboriginal Studies Press permission and AIATSIS does not provide GIS data. Sites should LINK to it rather than embed or redraw it.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: At colonisation there were more than 250 Indigenous languages including about 800 dialects; NILS3 (2018-19) found 123 still spoken, 109 endangered and 14 strong, with at least 31 being reawakened.
knowledge.label: evidence (figures via AIATSIS summary; verify exact wording on page before publishing)

knowledge.text: Anangu state that 'Dreamtime'/'Dreaming' suggests beliefs are unreal; Tjukurpa is not a dream and there is no word 'Dreamtime' in Anangu languages. Tjukurpa is the foundation of law, religion and morality.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Some Tjukurpa knowledge is passed only to people who have inherited the right to it; sacred objects, some designs and sounds (e.g. bullroarer) are restricted, sometimes by gender.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: AustLang assigns each language variety a stable alphanumeric code; the letter denotes a region (P = contact languages, T = Tasmanian), from Arthur Capell's 1963 scheme.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Pitjantjatjara (C6) and Yankunytjatjara (C4) are dialects of the Western Desert language (A80); many Pitjantjatjara people live with Yankunytjatjara at Amata, Ernabella, Fregon, Mimili and Indulkana.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Torres Strait Islanders are united by Tagai stories, which centre on the stars and identify them as sea people.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: 'Zenadth Kes' is a name used instead of 'Torres Strait', created by Elder and linguist Adhi Ephraim Bani from traditional names of the four winds.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Torres Strait Creole (P2) is shared across Zenadth Kes; Meriam Mir (Y3, eastern; a Papuan language) and Kala Lagaw Ya (Y1, western) are traditional languages under community-led revitalisation.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: TSRA supports 17 inhabited islands of the Torres Strait plus Bamaga and Seisia on the Northern Peninsula Area.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Erubam Le (Erub/Darnley Island) calendar Erub Kerker has 4 main seasons; Tagai's position signals voyaging, turtle mating, garden times, wind change and monsoon. Produced 2021 with Elders, Erubam Rangers and TSRA TEK team.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Masig (Yorke Island) seasonal calendar produced 2018 with Masigalgal RNTBC and Masigalgal Rangers; Masig is a small low-lying coral cay in the Central Islands about 160 km north-east of Thursday Island.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Nyoongar seasonal calendar has 6 seasons: Birak, Bunuru, Djeran, Makuru, Djilba and Kambarang.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Yawuru calendar (Broome, WA) has 6 seasons, e.g. Man-gala, the wet season (Dec-Mar).
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Jawoyn calendar (Katherine region, NT) has 5 seasons defined by weather and environment.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Maung calendar (Goulburn Islands, off Arnhem Land) explains plant and animal indicators of seasons.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Tiwi calendar recognises 3 major and 13 minor seasons.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Yanyuwa calendar (Gulf of Carpentaria) has 5 seasons, starting with Wunthurru, the early storm season.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Miriwoong calendar (Kununurra, WA) has 3 major seasons: hot, wet and cold.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Kaurna calendar (Adelaide Plains) recognises 4 weather periods plus seasonal-indicator winds; mapping to European months is approximate.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Brambuk seasonal cycle of Gariwerd (Grampians, Vic) recognises 6 seasons.
knowledge.label: evidence
knowledge.nation: Djab Wurrung / Jardwadjali (inference: nations of Gariwerd; not named in cited snippet)

knowledge.text: D'harawal Country and language area extends from the southern shores of Port Jackson toward the Shoalhaven River; BOM publishes a D'harawal seasonal calendar.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Banbai calendar relates to the 650 ha Wattleridge Indigenous Protected Area, NSW.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: At Kata Tjuta the ancestral beings' activities are so sensitive that not even their names can be revealed; it is a men's site and its Tjukurpa is not shared with visitors.
knowledge.label: evidence
knowledge.sensitivity: RESTRICTED - do not seek or publish stories

knowledge.text: palawa kani means 'Tasmanian Aborigines speak' and is the only Aboriginal language in lutruwita/Tasmania today; the TAC palawa kani Language Program has revived it since the early 1990s.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: palawa kani is a composite language revived from historical records of the original Tasmanian languages.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: AustLang lists historical Tasmanian varieties T1-T15, which with historical sources underpin palawa kani (T16); estimates of the original number of languages run from about 8 to 12.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: The TAC lists 16 gazetted Aboriginal or dual names in palawa kani, e.g. truwana (Cape Barren Island), kunanyi (Mt Wellington), kanamaluka (Tamar), takayna (Tarkine), larapuna (Bay of Fires), putalina (Oyster Cove).
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: lutruwita is the palawa kani name for Tasmania, revived from G.A. Robinson's records.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Arrernte (C8) covers Eastern and Central Arrernte, spoken in places including Mparntwe (Alice Springs), Santa Teresa and Harts Range; Alyawarr (C14) is a related Arandic language.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Warlpiri (C15; people call themselves Yapa); communities include Yuendumu, Lajamanu, Nyirrpi and Willowra.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: The ranges around Alice Springs are part of the caterpillar dreaming that tells how Mparntwe was formed; Anthwerrke (Emily Gap) is where the caterpillar songlines Yeperenye, Ntyarlke and Utnerrengatye intersect.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Anthwerrke (Emily Gap) is a registered sacred site; Traditional Owners ask visitors not to climb the rocks or photograph rock art.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Yalangbara (Port Bradshaw) is the most important site in north-east Arnhem Land for Dhuwa moiety people - the site of the first ancestors, the Djang'kawu.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Many Aboriginal artworks carry strict rules about who may paint certain symbols; students should not copy Aboriginal paintings or symbols.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: In 1963 Yolngu from Yirrkala sent the Yirrkala Bark Petitions, in Yolngu Matha and English, to Parliament, protesting the removal of land for bauxite mining; signatories represented clans of both moieties.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters was curated with senior custodians of Martu country and the APY and Ngaanyatjarra lands; it showed sections of five Western and Central Desert songlines across 500,000 km2.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: Papunya, 240 km west of Alice Springs, was founded in 1959; by 1970 about 1,400 people lived there - Pintupi, Luritja, Warlpiri, Kakatja and Anmatyerr.
knowledge.label: evidence

knowledge.text: In 1971 Papunya men began painting traditional designs on boards; Papunya Tula Artists (1972) was Australia's first Aboriginal arts company. Artists later changed styles to hide secret or sacred knowledge.
knowledge.label: evidence
knowledge.sensitivity: Early boards contained restricted designs - do not reproduce

knowledge.text: The Waugal (spellings include Waakal, Wagyl) is the major spirit for Noongar, a serpent recognised as giver of life maintaining all fresh water; it made Noongar custodians of the land and in the Nyitting created rivers, swamps and waterholes.
knowledge.label: evidence

stories.title: Kuniya and Liru (Tjukurpa)
stories.public_summary: Officially described as the battle between Kuniya (woma python woman) and Liru (poisonous brown snake man) at Mutitjulu Waterhole, which shaped Uluru; marks remain in the stone and the Cultural Centre building represents the two beings.
stories.label: evidence
stories.sensitivity: HIGH - Parks Australia explicitly asks people NOT to replicate or re-tell Tjukurpa stories, including names. RECOMMEND: do not publish a retelling; link to uluru.gov.au only, or seek permission via Anangu/Central Land Council.

stories.title: Budj Bim, the Ancestral Being and volcano
stories.public_summary: Gunditjmara tell that ancestors witnessed the eruption of the Budj Bim volcano, in which the Ancestral Being Budj Bim ('Big Head') revealed/transformed himself into the landscape; the lava flow later underpinned kooyang (short-finned eel) aquaculture built from at least 6,600 years ago.
stories.label: evidence
stories.uncertainty: Eruption dating varies by source: ~30,000 yrs (DCCEEW, Budj Bim site), 37,000 yrs (ORIC); UNESCO cites 'deep time' of at least 32,000 yrs.
stories.sensitivity: Publicly shared by Gunditjmara via their own site; quote summary only and credit Gunditjmara; check ICIP terms with GMTOAC before extended use.

stories.title: Tagai
stories.nation: Torres Strait Islanders (as told by Gail Mabo, Piadram clan, Mer)
stories.public_summary: Tagai is a figure in the stars: a man standing in a canoe holding a fishing spear (the Southern Cross) in his left hand and a sorbi fruit in his right. In one public version his 12 crew ate the voyage's food, so Tagai cast them into the sea and they became star patterns (Pleiades, Orion). Tagai guides navigation, planting, turtle and dugong hunting and seasons.
stories.label: evidence
stories.sensitivity: Publicly shared by knowledge holder; credit Gail Mabo and Mer; quote her own published words.
stories.deceased_note: Mentions the late Eddie Koiki Mabo and Benny Mabo - show deceased-persons warning.

stories.title: Bunjil at Gariwerd
stories.place: Bunjil's Shelter, Black Range Scenic Reserve near Stawell, Vic
stories.public_summary: Parks Victoria: Bunjils Shelter holds the only known rock-art depiction of the creator spirit Bunjil and is one of the most significant cultural places in south-eastern Australia. (Dingo-helper detail is from secondary sources only.)
stories.label: evidence (verified: Parks Victoria page read)
stories.sensitivity: Check with Barengi Gadjin Land Council / Eastern Maar on current wording.

stories.title: The Waugal (Waakal / Wagyl)
stories.place: Fresh waterways of Noongar boodja, incl. Darling Scarp (Derbarl Yerrigan link is search-summary only)
stories.public_summary: The Waugal is a serpent spirit recognised by Noongar as the giver of life, maintaining fresh water; in the Nyitting it created the rivers, swamps and waterholes, and it made Noongar custodians of the land. The Darling Scarp is said to represent its body.
stories.label: evidence (verified via archived Kaartdijin Noongar page)
stories.sensitivity: Community-published; credit Noongar and link to Kaartdijin Noongar.

stories.title: The Three Sisters (contested story) and Muggadah
stories.public_summary: The widely told 'legend' of the Three Sisters is traced to a 1931 newspaper story by schoolgirl Patricia Stone, later popularised by Mel Ward (1949). Gundungurra describe the formations as remnants of seven stone pillars linked to the Muggadah (Seven Sisters Dreaming, Pleiades). Declared an Aboriginal Place 2014.
stories.label: evidence
stories.sensitivity: Use as a teaching example of misattributed 'Dreaming' stories; do not present the tourist version as Aboriginal.
stories.deceased_note: Dictionary of Sydney cites the late Aunty Joan Cooper (Darug).

stories.title: The Caterpillar Dreaming of Mparntwe
stories.place: Anthwerrke (Emily Gap) and ranges around Alice Springs
stories.public_summary: Public park materials say the caterpillar beings of Mparntwe originated at Anthwerrke, formed the gap and many features around Alice Springs, and radiated out to the edge of the Simpson Desert. Three caterpillar songlines - Yeperenye, Ntyarlke and Utnerrengatye - intersect there.
stories.label: evidence
stories.sensitivity: Registered sacred site; Traditional Owners share fuller story via their Anthwerrke app - link there.

stories.title: Journey of the Djang'kawu to Yalangbara
stories.nation: Yolngu - Rirratjingu clan (Dhuwa moiety); custodians the Marika family
stories.public_summary: As published by the National Museum for schools: the Djang'kawu - two sisters and a male companion - travelled from Burralku to Yalangbara, where the Rirratjingu clan has its origin. The Marika family are custodians; Dhuwa moiety.
stories.label: evidence
stories.sensitivity: Published for education with the Marika family; do not copy associated artworks/symbols.
stories.deceased_persons: unknown - apply deceased-persons warning by default
stories.deceased_note: Resource names artists Mawalan and Milpirrum Marika - apply warning.

stories.title: Seven Sisters (Minyipuru / Kungkarangkalpa)
stories.place: Western and Central Deserts (e.g. Pangkal, Parnngurr, Walinynga/Cave Hill)
stories.public_summary: The Seven Sisters songlines are a story of pursuit and escape travelling west to east across Martu, Ngaanyatjarra and APY lands; NMA's exhibition was directed by senior custodians.
stories.label: evidence
stories.sensitivity: Much of the songline is restricted; publish only what NMA/custodians present publicly.
stories.deceased_persons: unknown - apply deceased-persons warning by default
